To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we derived a quantum theory of coherent energy transfer in arbitrary nanophotonic systems, we derived an ultimate efficiency bound $\eta_{\text{max}} = \frac{\Gamma_a}{\Gamma_d + \Gamma_a}$ that is independent of the quantum coherence between the donor and acceptors and that we showed the control of the spontaneous emission of the acceptor as a new design paradigm for enhancing the efficiency of coherent energy transfer.

the fundamental efficiency bound $\eta_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{\Gamma_{a}}{\Gamma_{d} + \Gamma_{a}}$ for coherent energy transfer can be exceeded by exploiting the dipolar orientations of the donor-acceptor pair.

we derived a fundamental bound on the efficiency of energy transfer from a donor to an acceptor atom in nanophotonic systems, and that the bound can be reached by controlling the spontaneous emission rate of the acceptor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of fundamental theory for energy transfer in nanosystems, with applications to the development of new nanophotonic devices.
the fundamental efficiency limits of coherent energy transfer between two nanophotonics systems.
the fundamental limits of coherent energy transfer in arbitrary nanophotonic systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have developed the most general quantum theory of energy transfer in nanosystems.
our theory predicts that the maximum energy transfer efficiency is limited by the spontaneous emission rate of the acceptor.
the efficiency bound is a fundamental limit that can only be reached in a coherent way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fundamental bound for energy transfer efficiency can be enhanced using mirrors.
the efficiency bound is a universal property of energy transfer in nanoscale systems, and the control of the spontaneous emission rate of the acceptor can be used to reach the ultimate bound.
the ultimate bound of efficiency is determined by the spontaneous emission rate of the donor, which can be increased by engineering the dipole orientations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spontaneous emission of the acceptor is the key to understanding the energy transfer efficiency.
the efficiency of energy transfer between two quantum systems is fundamentally bounded by the ratio of the acceptor to the donor spontaneous emission rates.
the efficiency bound for coherent and incoherently driven systems is fundamentally different.
